name: Soukous
story: The rumba-section groove Franco and TPOK Jazz built the Kinshasa sound on. Cuban son records arrived in 1940s Léopoldville, Congolese musicians heard their own music in them, and sent it back out in Lingala.

name: Sebene (Cavacha)
story: The dance-section shift every Congolese song races toward. Zaiko Langa Langa's drummer Meridjo codified the cavacha after hearing it in a Kinshasa bar — sixteenth hats driving, snare syncopated, guitars let loose.

name: Ndombolo
story: Faster, harder, more snare — the late-90s evolution of soukous behind Awilo Longomba, Koffi Olomidé, and Werrason. The hips move on every ghost note.

name: Coupé-Décalé
story: "Cut and run" — coined in the Ivorian diaspora around Douk Saga and DJ Arafat, built on ndombolo's skeleton and Parisian club production. When Arafat died in 2019, Abidjan shut down for his funeral.

name: Highlife (Nigeria)
story: The Igbo east's take on highlife — guitar-centred, horns on the side, and a bell pattern rolling under it all. Osadebe, Rex Lawson, Oliver De Coque wrote the book.

name: Jùjú
story: King Sunny Adé's African Beats could field three talking drums at once, a pedal steel shimmering over the top, and a choir underneath. The drum speaks Yoruba.

name: Fuji
story: Arguably the most percussion-dense popular music on earth — no guitars, no keyboards, just drums and voice. Born from Ramadan pre-dawn wake-up singing, named after a postcard of Mount Fuji.

name: Mbalax
story: Wolof sabar drumming translated into the pop band. The signature move: the strongest bass tones land just before 2 and 4, not on them — the rush that makes Youssou N'Dour's Super Étoile sound like it's leaning forward.

name: Makossa
story: Manu Dibango's "Soul Makossa" (1972) is the most sampled African song in history — Michael Jackson, Rihanna, and half of disco owe it royalties. The kick locks with the melodic Cameroonian bass and never lets go.

name: Bikutsi
story: "Beat the earth." A Beti women's music where the feet stomp the ground in galloping 6/8 triplets. Les Têtes Brûlées electrified it in the 1980s with shaved heads, painted bodies, and loud guitars.

name: Kwaito
story: House music dropped to township speed — 100-115 BPM, heavier, lazier, defiantly local. Born in Soweto the year apartheid ended. Arthur Mafokate, Mandoza, Brenda Fassie sang it into the new South Africa.

name: Gqom (Durban Broken)
story: Durban's stuttering answer to four-on-the-floor. Made on cracked software in Inanda and KwaMashu, shared taxi-to-taxi over Bluetooth. DJ Lag, Distruction Boyz, Rudeboyz. The kick refuses to land where you expect.

name: Shangaan Electro
story: Nozinja built a dance genre at 180-240 BPM for the Tsonga community in Limpopo — impossibly fast, bone-dry, built on layered hand-claps. The Shangaan footwork that goes with it has to be seen to be believed.

name: Mbaqanga
story: Mahlathini's grandfather-voice growl, the Mahotella Queens' tight harmonies, and the Makgona Tsohle Band's shuffling 4/4 underneath. "Steamed maize bread" in Zulu — humble, everyday, nourishing.

name: Maskandi
story: A Zulu troubadour tradition carried from KwaZulu-Natal into the mines of Johannesburg. Every piece opens with izihlabo — a free-tempo guitar cadenza — before the band finds this steady groove.

name: Benga
story: D.O. Misiani and Shirati Jazz translated the nyatiti lyre's cascading eight-string figures onto electric guitar. The drummer gives the cymbal a workout while the bass bubbles underneath.

name: Bongo Flava
story: Dar es Salaam's chart sound, filtered through American R&B production and taarab melody. Diamond Platnumz and the Wasafi camp turned the 3+3+2 kick into East Africa's default pop clock.

name: Gengetone
story: Nairobi's 2018 breakout — rapped in Sheng slang over dem-bow kicks and trap hats. Ethic Entertainment, Sailors Gang, Boondocks Gang: five or six vocalists trading bars with the crowd shouting back.

name: Kuduro
story: "Hard ass" — born in Luanda's musseques during the civil war, made on whatever hardware was around. Tony Amado glued house's four-on-the-floor to the tresillo snare and never looked back.

name: Semba
story: The Angolan dance — and the word — that crossed the Atlantic with enslaved people and evolved into Brazilian samba. The reco-reco scrape on top of this galloping groove is the same rhythmic DNA.

name: Kizomba
story: Slowed-down semba crossed with Antillean zouk, built for close partner dancing. The snare pulls gently on the "and" of two — the tiny hook everything else in the song leans on.

name: Funaná
story: An accordion and a scraped iron rod — that's the whole engine of funaná. The Portuguese colonial administration banned it as "primitive"; after independence in 1975 the Badiu of Santiago made it a national sound.

name: Morna
story: Cape Verde's soul music — sodade, the ache for a home you may never have seen. Cesária Évora sang it to the world barefoot. The percussion barely intrudes; the song does the work.

name: Singeli
story: Sisso, DJ Maiko, Bamba Pana — Dar es Salaam producers sped mchiriku and taarab to 200, 250, 300 BPM until the individual hits blur into texture. The Nyege Nyege Festival took it to Europe without slowing it down.

name: Afrobeats (Pon Pon)
story: Distinct from Fela's Afrobeat — the modern Nigerian chart template behind Wizkid, Burna Boy, Davido. Tekno's "Pana" codified the pon-pon log-drum bounce that now runs half of global pop.

name: Azonto
story: A 2011 Accra dance craze that went global on YouTube before "going viral" was a production category. The beat is a highlife skeleton wrapped in a bell timeline and cleaned up for export.

name: Amapiano Groove
story: The kick sits on the floor, the shaker counts half-notes, and the log drum bounces in the gaps. Kabza De Small and DJ Maphorisa built it from kwaito's tempo and deep-house's patience.

name: Zouglou
story: Ivorian university-campus protest music of the early 1990s — satire and frustration set to handclap-heavy grooves. Magic System's "Premier Gaou" took it out of the dorms and into every radio on the continent.
